## Why a second recording

`directxmath-336` is a **pure addition**: +221 −0. A comparison with no removed
line has no line to pair an added line against, so it cannot produce intraline
emphasis at any zoom, under any palette, on any host. Every capture taken from
it was therefore incapable of showing the word-level highlighting RFC-BPR-0004
specifies, and no reviewer has ever been shown it. That is BPR-0214, and it is
why this fixture exists rather than a wider crop of the old one.

The product owner designated this pull request for it.

## What makes it the right shape

Three modification pairs where the removed and added lines are nearly the same
text:

| file | shared | differs |
|---|---|---|
| `UIforETW/Resource.h` | 98% | 1 character |
| `UIforETW/UIforETW.rc` | 99% | 1 character |
| `UIforETW/UIforETW.rc` | 97% | 2 characters |

```
-#define _APS_NEXT_RESOURCE_VALUE        136
+#define _APS_NEXT_RESOURCE_VALUE        137
```

A one-character delta on an otherwise identical line is the clearest case
intraline emphasis has: whole-line background alone says "this line changed",
and only the word-level mark says *what* changed. If the emphasis is missing or
mis-registered, a capture of these rows shows it immediately.

It also keeps a plain addition-only file (`UIforETWDlg.cpp`, +22 −0) and a
mixed one, so a capture can hold added, removed and modified rows together
rather than needing three fixtures to compare them.

## Blobs, not just patches

Each file carries `base_content_base64` and `head_content_base64` — its whole
content on both sides — beside the patch.

That is not redundancy. The comparison surface diffs real file content out of
git objects; the served fixture's `responses/files.json` carries no patch at
all, and the content comes from git packfiles. A patch is hunks with context,
so the base and head of a file cannot be reconstructed from one. Without the
blobs this recording could be validated but never rendered, which is the gap
BPR-0187 records.

The blobs are checked against the recording rather than trusted: each pair is
diffed and must produce exactly the additions and deletions the API reported.
All five files reconstruct exactly. Two base64 strings that merely decode would
be evidence of nothing.

## `objects.pack`

The blobs built into git objects, which is the form the product can actually
read. Generated by `scripts/build_recorded_pull_request_pack.py`, which builds a
two-commit repository — base, then head — and packs it.

| | |
|---|---|
| base commit | `8b70ee179fe55b705ee4e613ecbc89a0acebc1bc` |
| head commit | `e40058be7d5fe319342dffb567ce30e42bc6f4de` |
| size | 32,229 bytes |

The commits are stable because the generator pins the author and committer
identity and both timestamps. Two runs produce byte-identical packs, which is
what lets a test name these identifiers instead of discovering them.

The generator refuses to write a pack whose diff does not reproduce the
recording's own additions and deletions, file by file. Running it against
`directxmath-336` fails, correctly, with *"Inc/DirectXMath.h is absent from the
built comparison"* — that recording has no blobs, so there is nothing to build.

## Recorded, not read live

Fetched once with three unauthenticated `GET`s — the pull request, its files,
its commits — then trimmed to what a review surface reads. A test that reaches
the network fails when the network does, and a fixture that changes when
somebody pushes to a branch is not a fixture.

Everything the API returns that a review surface has no use for was dropped:
avatars, node identifiers, reaction counts, and the URL fields on every object.

Grepping the recording finds three URLs rather than one. Two are inside the
diff text — `msdn.microsoft.com` links in comments the pull request itself adds
— so they are reviewed content, not API metadata. Outside the patches the
provenance line is the only URL, and the validator holds that distinction rather
than counting URLs in the file as a whole.

**No credential is involved.** These are unauthenticated reads of public data,
and nothing here is written back.

## What is served, and what is not

This recording is now served through the public path as
`--github-fixture uiforetw-74`. The contract tree under
`tests/fixtures/github/contracts/v1/uiforetw-74/` is generated from this file
by `scripts/build_recorded_pull_request_contract.py`; it is not edited by hand,
and `recorded_pull_request_fixture_tests.py` regenerates it into a temporary
directory and compares bytes so the two cannot drift.

**The commit identifiers the product serves are not the ones recorded here.**

| | recorded above | served |
|---|---|---|
| base | `7c519e97eb906bdc6b83c8f576c91c063d6ceee9` | `8b70ee179fe55b705ee4e613ecbc89a0acebc1bc` |
| head | `9b01c587b3e46637ff69c3801841993bd054f106` | `e40058be7d5fe319342dffb567ce30e42bc6f4de` |

The served pair are the commits `build_recorded_pull_request_pack.py` builds
from the blobs recorded here into `objects.pack`. GitHub's real commits cannot
be reproduced from this recording: a commit OID hashes its trees, parents and
author records, and none of those were recorded — a patch is hunks with
context, not whole objects. The product owner decided on 2026-08-08 to serve
the generated pair and document the divergence rather than grow the recording,
which would have meant committing a clone of the repository.

The recorded OIDs above are still asserted. They are what a re-fetch is checked
against, so a drifted re-fetch fails rather than silently changing content a
presentation judgement was made against. They are also asserted to appear
*nowhere* under `contracts/v1/`, because serving a real OID beside a pack built
from generated ones is the state that connects and then fails at import.
